editorial:
Ever wonder how a movie can cause a total riot before it even hits theaters? You get a front-row seat to that chaos in this documentary. It takes you back to the late 70s and early 80s to show how William Friedkin tried to make a gritty crime thriller about the underground gay scene in New York City. You will see old footage, hear from the crew, and feel the tension as the filmmakers clash with angry protesters who hated the script. It feels less like a boring history lesson and more like a fly-on-the-wall look at a movie production falling apart in real time.

What really works here is how it shows the messy side of filmmaking. You get to see the struggle between art and politics without any fancy talk. The pacing is solid, though some of the interviews might feel a bit long if you aren't into movie trivia. If you love behind-the-scenes drama, you should definitely check this out. You can rent it on Apple TV for a quick watch, but if you are a real cinema fan, adding the 4K Blu-ray to your physical collection is the way to go for the best picture quality.
endingExplained: The documentary wraps up by showing how the movie was finally released despite the massive protests. It explains that the film never really found its footing with the public because it was too controversial for some and too slow for others. You see how the backlash ended up overshadowing the actual story. In the end, it concludes that the movie became a time capsule of the hate and fear present in society during that era.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves movie history and true stories about Hollywood drama.
